USMLE-style practice · Pharmacology

Separating ulcer prevention from obstetric use

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A student reads that misoprostol can be used by obstetric clinicians and concludes it is therefore safe for routine ulcer prevention in any pregnant patient. Which distinction best corrects this reasoning?

  1. Ulcer prophylaxis requires higher doses than every obstetric use
  2. A uterotonic effect may be deliberately used in one indication but hazardous in another
  3. Pregnancy eliminates the drug's uterine effects
  4. The gastric formulation has no systemic activity
  5. Only intravenous prostaglandins affect the uterus
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

A uterotonic effect may be deliberately used in one indication but hazardous in another

Indication, gestational context and supervision matter; intentional obstetric use does not make NSAID-ulcer prophylaxis safe in pregnancy.

Understanding the options

A uterotonic effect may be deliberately used in one indication but hazardous in another
Indication, gestational context and supervision matter; intentional obstetric use does not make NSAID-ulcer prophylaxis safe in pregnancy.
Pregnancy eliminates the drug's uterine effects
Pregnancy does not remove uterine responsiveness.
The gastric formulation has no systemic activity
Oral misoprostol is systemically active.
Only intravenous prostaglandins affect the uterus
Nonintravenous administration can have uterotonic effects.
Ulcer prophylaxis requires higher doses than every obstetric use
Comparing all doses does not establish safety and is not universally valid.
